title: Welcome and Table of Contents
summary: What SS1 Financial Accounting Third Term is about, how to use the notes, and a map of every unit.

p: In Second Term you prepared the trading account and the profit and loss account. In Third Term you complete the picture with the balance sheet, which shows what the business owns and owes at the end of the year. You also learn how large businesses keep control of their many debtors and creditors with control accounts, how to spread the cost of assets over their lives (depreciation), and how a factory works out the cost of the goods it makes (the manufacturing account).

Accounting is learned by doing. Copy each worked example in your notebook, cover the answer and try again. At the end of every unit are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.

title: The Balance Sheet: Meaning, Purpose and the Accounting Equation
summary: What a balance sheet is, why it is prepared, the accounting equation and how transactions affect it.

p: A balance sheet is a financial statement that shows the financial position of a business at a particular date by listing its assets, liabilities and capital. It is also called the statement of financial position or the position statement.

Key points: it shows what the business owns (assets); it shows what the business owes (liabilities); it shows the owner's interest (capital); it is prepared at a point in time, so the heading is 'as at 31 December 2024' and NOT 'for the year ended' (that is for the profit and loss account); it is the last of the financial statements; and it is not part of the double entry.

1. To show the financial position: the assets, the debts and the net worth. 2. To show the ability to pay debts (solvency and liquidity). 3. To help decisions on investment, lending and expansion. 4. To judge performance by looking at the growth of assets and capital and the level of debt. 5. To meet legal requirements: the Companies Act and tax rules. 6. To provide a basis for analysis and for comparing years and businesses. 7. To inform the owners, banks, investors, creditors and the government.

Assets = Capital + Liabilities. Rearranged, Capital = Assets − Liabilities. The equation must always balance. Assets are the resources the business owns. Capital is the owner's investment. Liabilities are amounts owed to outsiders. The business uses the owner's capital and borrowed money to buy its assets.
Example 2: capital ₦400,000, liabilities ₦150,000. Assets = ₦550,000.
Owner introduces more capital ₦50,000: cash (an asset) rises by ₦50,000 and capital rises by ₦50,000. The equation still balances.
Bought goods on credit ₦30,000: stock (an asset) rises by ₦30,000 and creditors (a liability) rise by ₦30,000.
Paid a creditor ₦20,000: cash falls by ₦20,000 and creditors fall by ₦20,000.

title: Classification of Items, Order of Arrangement and Working Capital
summary: Fixed assets and current assets, current and long-term liabilities, capital, the order of arrangement, balance sheet compared with trial balance and working capital.

p: Fixed (non-current) assets are used in the business for more than a year and are not meant for resale. Examples: land, buildings, machinery, motor vehicles, furniture and fittings, equipment, computers, goodwill, patents and trademarks. They are shown at cost less accumulated depreciation, which is the net book value. (Land is not usually depreciated.)
Current assets are short-term assets that change all the time and can be turned into cash within a year: stock, debtors, prepayments, bank, cash, short-term investments and bills receivable.
Current liabilities are due within one year: creditors, bank overdraft, outstanding (accrued) expenses, short-term loans, bills payable and tax owing.
Long-term (non-current) liabilities are due after more than one year: long-term loans, mortgages, debentures and bonds.
Closing capital = opening capital + additional capital + net profit − drawings (− net loss). It belongs to the owner.

Fixed assets are listed by permanence: the most permanent first (land, buildings, plant and machinery, motor vehicles, furniture and fittings, equipment). Current assets are listed by liquidity (how easily they turn into cash): least liquid first, so stock, debtors, prepayments, bank and then cash. The reason is that stock is sold on credit to give debtors, who pay and so give cash. Current liabilities are listed by urgency, such as overdraft, creditors, outstanding expenses and short-term loans. Some businesses use the reverse order. Both are acceptable if you are consistent.

p: Working capital (net current assets) = current assets − current liabilities. It measures the ability to pay short-term debts and run day-to-day business.

Example: stock ₦50,000, debtors ₦80,000, bank ₦30,000, cash ₦10,000 give current assets of ₦170,000. Creditors ₦60,000 and outstanding expenses ₦10,000 give current liabilities of ₦70,000. Working capital = 170,000 − 70,000 = ₦100,000. A positive amount means the business can pay its short-term debts and still have funds to operate. Negative working capital (current liabilities greater than current assets) suggests liquidity problems.

title: Preparing a Balance Sheet: Steps and Formats
summary: The six steps for preparing a balance sheet and the horizontal and vertical formats.

p: Step 1: identify the items: separate assets from liabilities and find the capital items and any adjustments. Step 2: classify them: fixed assets, current assets, current liabilities, long-term liabilities and capital. Step 3: calculate the capital: opening capital + additional capital + net profit − drawings − net loss. Step 4: arrange the items in order: fixed assets by permanence, current assets by liquidity, liabilities by urgency. Step 5: calculate the totals, the working capital and the net assets, and check that the equation balances. Step 6: present the statement neatly with a heading, 'as at' date, clear labels and ruled lines.
The left side shows capital and liabilities (the sources of funds). The right side shows the assets (the uses of funds). Both sides must total the same amount.

p: The assets and liabilities come first and give the net assets, which must equal the capital shown under 'financed by'.

p: The top part of the vertical format shows the assets and liabilities. The bottom part shows the capital. The net assets must equal the capital. If they do not, there is an error somewhere.

title: Worked Examples, Special Items and Common Errors
summary: Three corrected balance sheets (Tunde, Aduke and Bisi), how special items such as prepayments and overdrafts are treated, and ten common errors.

p: Balances at 31 December 2024: net profit for the year ₦60,000; drawings ₦25,000; land ₦100,000; buildings ₦80,000; motor vehicles ₦50,000; furniture ₦30,000; stock ₦40,000; debtors ₦55,000; bank ₦28,000; cash ₦5,000; creditors ₦45,000; loan (repayable 2027) ₦30,000.

Fixed assets ₦260,000. Current assets ₦128,000 (40,000 + 55,000 + 28,000 + 5,000). Total assets ₦388,000. Current liabilities ₦45,000 and long-term liability ₦30,000: total ₦75,000. So the capital must be 388,000 − 75,000 = ₦313,000 at the end. That means the opening capital must have been ₦278,000 (313,000 − 60,000 + 25,000). Your notes give opening capital of ₦150,000, which leaves the balance sheet ₦128,000 out. The correct opening capital is ₦278,000.

Trial balance (debit): drawings 30,000; premises 150,000; motor vehicles 80,000; furniture 50,000; stock (1 January) 40,000; purchases 180,000; carriage inwards 6,000; debtors 60,000; bank 25,000; cash 4,000; salaries 50,000; rent 20,000; insurance 8,000; discount allowed 3,000. Credit: sales 320,000; creditors 48,000; discount received 2,000; provision for depreciation, motor vehicles 16,000 and furniture 10,000; provision for bad debts 3,000; capital. Adjustments: closing stock ₦48,000; depreciate motor vehicles 20% and furniture 10%; provision for bad debts at 5% of debtors.
The debits total ₦706,000 and the credits without capital total ₦399,000, so the capital must be ₦307,000 (your notes show ₦200,000 and a trial balance that did not agree).

Trading account: sales 320,000; cost of goods sold 40,000 + 180,000 + 6,000 − 48,000 = 178,000; gross profit ₦142,000. Profit and loss: gross profit 142,000 + discount received 2,000 = 144,000; expenses salaries 50,000, rent 20,000, insurance 8,000, discount allowed 3,000, depreciation of motor vehicles 16,000 and furniture 5,000 = 102,000; net profit ₦42,000. The provision for bad debts is 5% of 60,000 = 3,000, the same as before, so no charge.

head: Aduke Traders: balance sheet at 31 December 2024

p: Net profit ₦85,000; drawings ₦40,000; land ₦200,000; buildings cost ₦150,000 (provision ₦30,000); motor vehicles cost ₦120,000 (provision ₦40,000); furniture cost ₦60,000 (provision ₦18,000); stock ₦65,000; debtors ₦90,000 (provision ₦4,500); bank ₦35,000; cash ₦8,000; creditors ₦70,000; outstanding salaries ₦12,000; prepaid insurance ₦5,000; loan (repayable 2028) ₦80,000.

Fixed assets: 200,000 + 120,000 + 80,000 + 42,000 = ₦442,000. Current assets: stock 65,000, debtors net 85,500, prepaid insurance 5,000, bank 35,000, cash 8,000 = ₦198,500. Current liabilities 70,000 + 12,000 = ₦82,000. Net current assets ₦116,500. Less loan ₦80,000. Net assets ₦478,500.

Closing capital must be ₦478,500. So opening capital = 478,500 − 85,000 + 40,000 = ₦433,500. Your notes give ₦300,000, which leaves a ₦133,500 gap; the opening capital in the question should be ₦433,500 (or ₦133,500 of additional capital must have been introduced).

Depreciation: cost less provision for depreciation = net book value. Provision for bad debts: debtors less provision = net debtors. Accrued income (income receivable), such as rent receivable: a current asset. Accrued expenses (outstanding), such as wages owing: a current liability. Prepayments: a current asset. Income received in advance: a current liability. Bank overdraft: always a current liability. Additional capital: added to opening capital before the profit. Net loss: deducted from capital.
Example with additional capital: opening capital ₦100,000 + additional capital ₦50,000 = ₦150,000; + profit ₦30,000 = ₦180,000; − drawings ₦20,000 = closing capital ₦160,000.

1. Stock under fixed assets (it is a current asset). 2. Wrong order (cash before stock). 3. Forgetting depreciation. 4. Forgetting drawings in the capital. 5. Showing an overdraft as an asset. 6. Not deducting the provision from debtors. 7. Not checking that the equation balances. 8. Writing 'for the year ended' instead of 'as at'. 9. Including nominal accounts (expenses and income). 10. Poor presentation.
